title: Imitation, Inverse, Multi-agent and Safe RL
oneLiner: What changes when you learn from demonstrations instead of rewards, infer goals from behaviour, share the world with other learners, or must respect safety limits.

what.html:
Real problems bend the basic RL setting. Imitation learning copies an expert's actions; inverse RL works out what the expert was trying to achieve; preference learning learns a reward from "this one's better" comparisons. Multi-agent RL has several learners affecting each other. Safe RL maximises reward while keeping costs (collisions, energy) under a limit.

Everyday versionA learner driver who only copies a driving teacher's moves (imitation) gets into trouble the first time they drift somewhere the teacher never went; a teacher who says what to do in those moments (DAgger) fixes that.

why.html:
• Writing a good reward is hard; demonstrations and comparisons are easier to give.
  • Traffic, markets and games all involve many agents.
  • Robots, cars and chatbots need limits, not just high scores.

how.title: Copy the expert
how.html: Behavioural cloning trains a classifier: given the state, predict the expert's action. If the policy gives the expert's action 80% probability the loss is 0.223; 20% gives 1.609.

how.title: The drift problem and DAgger
how.html: A copier that drifts slightly ends up in situations the expert never showed, makes bigger mistakes and drifts further. DAgger lets the learner drive, asks the expert what to do in the places the learner actually went, and retrains.

how.title: Work out the goal
how.html: Inverse RL guesses the reward that makes the expert's behaviour sensible, then optimises it. Many rewards fit, so the aim is a useful one. GAIL skips the reward: it trains the policy until a judge can't tell it apart from the expert.

how.title: Rewards from comparisons
how.html: Show a person two short clips and ask which is better. A reward model learns to agree with those choices; RL then optimises it. The same idea powers RLHF for chatbots.

how.title: Many agents at once
how.html: Each agent's world keeps changing because the others are learning too. The number of joint actions explodes (5 actions and 8 agents give 390,625 combinations), and a shared team reward hides who did the good work.

how.title: Train together, act alone
how.html: During training, a critic can look at everyone's information; at deployment each agent acts on what it can see. MADDPG, QMIX and MAPPO all use this idea.

how.title: Reward with limits
how.html: Maximise reward while keeping expected cost below a budget. A penalty weight λ grows whenever the limit is broken, pushing the policy back. Always report violations and worst cases, not just average reward.

how.title: Where it's used, and a warning
how.html: Robots, driving, power grids, recommendations, finance, chatbots and coding agents. Whatever score you optimise, the agent may find a loophole (like editing the tests so they pass), so check the real outcome too.

demo.html: Drive with the cloned policy and watch it wander off the road once it drifts. Then run a DAgger iteration: the expert labels the places the learner actually went, and the new policy recovers.

example.html:
Safe RL in three actions. Action A pays 1.0 but costs 0.9; B pays 0.6 and costs 0.3; C pays 0.2 for free. With a cost budget of 0.3, the best you can do is B (0.6). The Lagrangian method first grabs A, breaks the budget, raises its penalty λ, and ends up on B exactly at the limit.

Supplementary The temporary violations during learning matter for real systems: safe exploration is its own research area.

misunderstandings: Good accuracy on expert data means good driving.
Distribution shift: errors compound off the expert's path.
Inverse RL recovers the one true reward.
Many rewards explain the same behaviour.
Multi-agent RL is just single-agent RL n times.
Other learners make each agent's environment non-stationary.
takeaways: BC: supervised imitation (losses 0.223 vs 1.609); suffers distribution shift.
IRL/MaxEnt IRL/GAIL/preferences learn from humans without a written reward.
MARL: non-stationarity, mⁿ joint actions, credit assignment; CTDE.
Safe RL: max J_R s.t. J_C ≤ d; proxy rewards get gamed.
thirty: Behavioural cloning learns a policy by supervised learning on expert (state, action) pairs, minimising −log πθ(aᴱ|s) (0.223 at probability 0.8, 1.609 at 0.2), but distribution shift makes errors compound; DAgger collects expert labels on learner-visited states and retrains. Inverse RL infers a (non-unique) reward explaining demonstrations, MaxEnt IRL makes higher-reward trajectories exponentially more likely, GAIL matches the expert's occupancy adversarially, and preference models learn rewards from comparisons. Multi-agent RL uses Markov games and faces non-stationarity, mⁿ joint actions, credit assignment and partial observability; centralised training with decentralised execution (MADDPG, QMIX, MAPPO) is standard. Safe RL maximises J_R subject to J_C ≤ d via Lagrangian methods, constrained optimisation, shielding or human intervention, and must report violations and tails. Learned rewards and verifiers are proxies that agents can exploit.

check.q: DAgger fixes BC's distribution shift by…
check.why: Aggregate expert labels on learner states.

check.q: 5 actions per agent, 4 agents: joint actions?

opts: Reward subject to a cost budget
